title: Parallelize multi-arch builds in release workflow
description:
Current release workflow builds images sequentially (amd64+arm64 for operator, then data-provider).
ARM64 builds are very slow due to QEMU emulation.

## Current Performance
- Operator build (amd64+arm64): ~15-20min
- Data-provider build (amd64+arm64): ~10-15min
- **Total: ~30min**

## Goal
Parallelize builds to reduce total time to ~15min or less.

## Current Workflow Structure
```yaml
jobs:
  build-and-push:
    steps:
      - Build operator (amd64+arm64)     # Sequential!
      - Build data-provider (amd64+arm64) # Sequential!
      - Create GitHub release
```

## Problem Analysis
1. **Sequential builds**: operator → data-provider
2. **Sequential platforms**: amd64 → arm64 (QEMU slow)
3. **Single runner**: all work on one machine

## Parallelization Strategies

### Strategy 1: Matrix Build (Recommended)
**Parallelization**: 4 jobs (2 images × 2 architectures)

```yaml
jobs:
  build:
    strategy:
      matrix:
        image: [operator, data-provider]
        platform: [linux/amd64, linux/arm64]
    steps:
      - Build single-platform image
      
  create-manifest:
    needs: build
    steps:
      - Create multi-arch manifests
      - Create GitHub release
```

**Pros**:
- ✅ Maximum parallelization (4 concurrent jobs)
- ✅ Each job builds only one platform
- ✅ Can use native ARM64 runners for faster ARM builds
- ✅ Independent job failures

**Cons**:
- ⚠️ More complex manifest creation
- ⚠️ Requires 4× GitHub Actions minutes (but finishes faster)

**Expected time**: ~10-12min (longest job = ARM64 build)

### Strategy 2: Parallel Images with Multi-Arch
**Parallelization**: 2 jobs (operator + data-provider in parallel)

```yaml
jobs:
  build-operator:
    steps:
      - Build operator (amd64+arm64)
      
  build-data-provider:
    steps:
      - Build data-provider (amd64+arm64)
      
  create-release:
    needs: [build-operator, build-data-provider]
    steps:
      - Create GitHub release
```

**Pros**:
- ✅ Simple to implement
- ✅ Less manifest complexity
- ✅ 2× parallelization

**Cons**:
- ⚠️ Still using QEMU for ARM64 (slow)
- ⚠️ Only 2 jobs instead of 4

**Expected time**: ~15-18min (longest of operator or data-provider)

### Strategy 3: Native ARM64 Runners (Advanced)
**Use GitHub ARM64 runners for ARM builds**

```yaml
jobs:
  build-amd64:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    strategy:
      matrix:
        image: [operator, data-provider]
    steps:
      - Build amd64
      
  build-arm64:
    runs-on: ubuntu-24.04-arm64  # Native ARM runner
    strategy:
      matrix:
        image: [operator, data-provider]
    steps:
      - Build arm64 (native, no QEMU!)
```

**Pros**:
- ✅ Native ARM64 build (10x faster than QEMU)
- ✅ Maximum performance
- ✅ 4 parallel jobs

**Cons**:
- ⚠️ Requires ARM64 runner availability
- ⚠️ May cost more (ARM runners pricing)

**Expected time**: ~8-10min (ARM builds native speed)

### Strategy 4: Hybrid - AMD64 Always, ARM64 on Tag
**Build ARM64 only for releases**

```yaml
# PR/push: AMD64 only (fast)
# Tags: AMD64 + ARM64 (slower but acceptable for releases)
```

**Pros**:
- ✅ Fast CI for development
- ✅ Full multi-arch only when needed

**Cons**:
- ⚠️ No ARM64 testing until release

## Recommended Implementation: Strategy 1 (Matrix)

### Workflow Structure
```yaml
name: Release

on:
  push:
    tags:
      - 'v*'

jobs:
  build-images:
    name: Build ${{ matrix.image }} - ${{ matrix.platform }}
    runs-on: ubuntu-24.04
    strategy:
      matrix:
        image: [operator, data-provider]
        platform: [linux/amd64, linux/arm64]
    steps:
      - name: Checkout
        uses: actions/checkout@v4

      - name: Set up QEMU
        if: matrix.platform == 'linux/arm64'
        uses: docker/setup-qemu-action@v3

      - name: Set up Docker Buildx
        uses: docker/setup-buildx-action@v3

      - name: Login to Quay.io
        uses: docker/login-action@v3
        with:
          registry: quay.io
          username: ${{ secrets.QUAY_USERNAME }}
          password: ${{ secrets.QUAY_PASSWORD }}

      - name: Set version
        run: echo "VERSION=${GITHUB_REF#refs/tags/}" >> $GITHUB_ENV

      - name: Build and push
        uses: docker/build-push-action@v6
        with:
          context: ${{ matrix.image == 'operator' && '.' || './krkn-operator-data-provider' }}
          platforms: ${{ matrix.platform }}
          push: true
          tags: |
            quay.io/krkn-chaos/krkn-${{ matrix.image }}:${{ env.VERSION }}-${{ matrix.platform == 'linux/amd64' && 'amd64' || 'arm64' }}
          cache-from: type=gha
          cache-to: type=gha,mode=max

  create-manifests:
    name: Create Multi-Arch Manifests
    needs: build-images
    runs-on: ubuntu-24.04
    steps:
      - name: Login to Quay.io
        uses: docker/login-action@v3
        with:
          registry: quay.io
          username: ${{ secrets.QUAY_USERNAME }}
          password: ${{ secrets.QUAY_PASSWORD }}

      - name: Set version
        run: echo "VERSION=${GITHUB_REF#refs/tags/}" >> $GITHUB_ENV

      - name: Create operator manifest
        run: |
          docker buildx imagetools create -t quay.io/krkn-chaos/krkn-operator:$VERSION \
            quay.io/krkn-chaos/krkn-operator:$VERSION-amd64 \
            quay.io/krkn-chaos/krkn-operator:$VERSION-arm64
          
          docker buildx imagetools create -t quay.io/krkn-chaos/krkn-operator:latest \
            quay.io/krkn-chaos/krkn-operator:$VERSION-amd64 \
            quay.io/krkn-chaos/krkn-operator:$VERSION-arm64

      - name: Create data-provider manifest
        run: |
          docker buildx imagetools create -t quay.io/krkn-chaos/krkn-operator-data-provider:$VERSION \
            quay.io/krkn-chaos/krkn-operator-data-provider:$VERSION-amd64 \
            quay.io/krkn-chaos/krkn-operator-data-provider:$VERSION-arm64
          
          docker buildx imagetools create -t quay.io/krkn-chaos/krkn-operator-data-provider:latest \
            quay.io/krkn-chaos/krkn-operator-data-provider:$VERSION-amd64 \
            quay.io/krkn-chaos/krkn-operator-data-provider:$VERSION-arm64

      - name: Create GitHub Release
        env:
          GH_TOKEN: ${{ github.token }}
        run: |
          # ... (same as current)
```

## Implementation Checklist

### Phase 1: Matrix Build Setup
- [ ] Create matrix strategy for images and platforms
- [ ] Update build steps to use matrix variables
- [ ] Add platform-specific tags (VERSION-amd64, VERSION-arm64)
- [ ] Enable GitHub Actions cache for builds

### Phase 4: Testing

- [ ] Measure actual time savings

### Phase 5: Optimization (Optional)
- [ ] Investigate native ARM64 runners (if available)
- [ ] Add build cache optimization
- [ ] Consider ARM64 only for releases (not PRs)

## Expected Results

**Before**:
- Total time: ~30 minutes
- Sequential execution
- Single runner bottleneck

**After (Matrix)**:
- Total time: ~12-15 minutes (50% faster)
- 4 parallel builds
- Better resource utilization

**After (Native ARM64)**:
- Total time: ~8-10 minutes (65% faster)
- Native ARM performance
- Maximum parallelization

## Risks & Mitigation

**Risk**: More GitHub Actions minutes consumed
- **Mitigation**: Faster execution = less total wall time, similar minute usage

**Risk**: Manifest creation complexity
- **Mitigation**: Use docker buildx imagetools (built-in support)

**Risk**: Intermittent failures in parallel jobs
- **Mitigation**: Add retry logic, fail-fast: false

## Measurement

Track before/after:
- [ ] Total workflow time
- [ ] Individual job times
- [ ] GitHub Actions minutes consumed
- [ ] Image size and layers

title: Consider email case normalization in Register/CreateUser
description:
Currently UserID (email) is stored case-sensitive but duplicate check is case-insensitive. This creates inconsistency:
  
- User registers 'Admin@Example.com'
- System saves literally 'Admin@Example.com'  
- Login must match exactly 'Admin@Example.com' (not 'admin@example.com')

Improvement: normalize email to lowercase at save time (req.UserID = strings.ToLower(req.UserID)) after ValidateEmail in both Register and CreateUser handlers.

Benefits:
- Consistent lookup (emails are case-insensitive per RFC)
- Better UX (no confusion about case variants)
- Simplifies duplicate check (can go back to case-sensitive)

Related to PR #30 review feedback.

description:
krkn-operator needs to follow the same pattern as krkn-operator-acm:
- Single controller that contributes for itself AND manages completion logic
- No separate "coordinator" or "contributor" roles - this distinction doesn't exist
- Just like ACM: contribute, count, mark completed, cleanup

## Current Situation (WRONG)

**Two separate controllers** (invented pattern, not required):
1. `KrknOperatorTargetProviderConfigReconciler` - only counts/marks completed
2. `ProviderConfigContributorReconciler` - only contributes (creates ConfigMap + JSON schema)

**Problem**:
- Fragile separation that was invented, not designed

title: [WebSocket v2] Per-run detail endpoint /api/v2/ws/runs/{scenarioRunName}
description:
## Context

The current WebSocket architecture has two levels:
1. **List-level** (`/api/v2/ws/runs`) — lightweight status updates (phase, counters) for all runs
2. **Log streaming** (`/api/v2/ws/scenarios/run/{name}/jobs/{id}/logs`) — raw log stream per job

The list-level endpoint intentionally does NOT send `clusterJobs` content to keep payloads small and avoid broadcasting heavy data to all connected clients. However, when a user expands a run accordion in the UI, they need the full run detail including all `clusterJobs` and their real-time status updates.

Currently the frontend falls back to a one-shot REST call (`GET /api/v1/scenarios/run/{scenarioRunName}`) to load `clusterJobs` on accordion open, but this creates poor UX: job statuses go stale immediately and the user must manually refresh to see updates.

## Requirement

Implement a **per-run detail WebSocket endpoint** that streams the full `ScenarioRunStatusResponse` (including `clusterJobs` array) for a single run.

### Endpoint

```
ws://host/api/v2/ws/runs/{scenarioRunName}
```

### Authentication

Same as existing v2 WebSocket endpoints: JWT via subprotocol `access_token.{token}`.

### Behavior

1. **On connect + subscribe**: Send an initial snapshot with the full current state of the run, including all `clusterJobs` with their current phases.

2. **On change**: Push an updated `ScenarioRunStatusResponse` whenever:
   - The run phase changes (e.g., Running → Succeeded)
   - Any `clusterJob` phase changes (e.g., Pending → Running → Succeeded/Failed)
   - A new `clusterJob` is created for this run
   - Job counters change (successfulJobs, failedJobs, runningJobs)

3. **On run deletion**: Send a `deleted` event and close the connection.

### Data Model

The response should match the existing `ScenarioRunStatusResponse` structure:

```json
{
  "resource": "run-detail",
  "id": "{scenarioRunName}",
  "event": "updated",
  "data": {
    "scenarioRunName": "my-scenario-abc123",
    "scenarioName": "my-scenario",
    "phase": "Running",
    "totalTargets": 3,
    "successfulJobs": 1,
    "failedJobs": 0,
    "runningJobs": 2,
    "clusterJobs": [
      {
        "providerName": "krkn-operator",
        "clusterName": "cluster-1",
        "jobId": "uuid-1",
        "podName": "pod-name-1",
        "phase": "Succeeded",
        "startTime": "2026-07-27T10:00:00Z",
        "completionTime": "2026-07-27T10:05:00Z",
        "containerImage": "quay.io/user/repo:tag"
      },
      {
        "providerName": "krkn-operator",
        "clusterName": "cluster-2",
        "jobId": "uuid-2",
        "podName": "pod-name-2",
        "phase": "Running",
        "startTime": "2026-07-27T10:01:00Z",
        "containerImage": "quay.io/user/repo:tag"
      }
    ],
    "createdAt": "2026-07-27T10:00:00Z",
    "ownerUserId": "user@example.com",
    "registryName": "my-registry",
    "graphRunName": "graph-run-xyz",
    "graphNodeId": "node-1"
  }
}
```

### ClusterJob fields (all required except noted):
- `providerName` (string) — Provider that owns the cluster
- `clusterName` (string) — Cluster name
- `jobId` (string) — UUID
- `podName` (string) — Pod name
- `phase` (string) — One of: Pending, Running, Succeeded, Failed
- `startTime` (string, optional) — ISO 8601
- `completionTime` (string, optional) — ISO 8601
- `message` (string, optional) — Error message on failure
- `containerImage` (string, optional) — Full image path

### Frontend lifecycle

- **Connect**: When user opens a run accordion (expands row)
- **Disconnect**: When user closes the accordion (collapses row)
- **Multiple connections**: A user may have 2-3 accordions open simultaneously; each is an independent connection
- **Short-lived**: Most connections last seconds to minutes (while user views a run)

### Message protocol

Same subscription pattern as existing endpoints:

Client → Server:
```json
{"action": "subscribe", "resource": "run-detail", "ids": ["{scenarioRunName}"]}
```

Server → Client:
```json
{"resource": "run-detail", "id": "{scenarioRunName}", "event": "updated|created|deleted", "data": {...}}
```

## Implementation notes

- Use the same Hub/Client/Broadcaster pattern from the existing v2 WebSocket implementation
- The Informer watcher should watch the specific ScenarioRun CR + its child Jobs
- Consider using the cache fingerprint approach to avoid broadcasting unchanged state
- The `clusterJobs` array must be complete on every update (not delta/patch)
- When the run reaches a terminal phase (Succeeded, Failed, PartiallyFailed), send a final update and the client will disconnect

## Relationship to existing endpoints

| Endpoint | Scope | Data | Lifetime |
|----------|-------|------|----------|
| `/api/v2/ws/runs` | All runs | Status only (no clusterJobs) | Always connected on jobs_list |
| `/api/v2/ws/runs/{name}` | Single run | Full detail + clusterJobs | While accordion open |
| `/api/v2/ws/.../logs` | Single job | Raw log stream | While LogViewer open |

## Acceptance criteria

1. Initial snapshot includes full `clusterJobs` array on connect
2. Real-time updates push when any `clusterJob` phase changes
3. Multiple simultaneous connections to different runs work correctly
4. Auth via subprotocol (same as existing)
5. Run deletion triggers `deleted` event

**Backend** (commit cb1934c):
- Added 'run-detail' resource type to existing `/api/v2/ws/runs` endpoint  
- Broadcasts full ScenarioRunStatusResponse with clusterJobs array
- Separate cache keys to avoid collision with lightweight broadcasts
- Files: handler.go (+67), broadcaster.go (+53), response_helpers.go (+22), watcher.go (+6)

title: WebSocket authentication via Sec-WebSocket-Protocol subprotocol
description:
**CORREZIONE: Implementazione WebSocket Auth Subprotocol**

Implement secure JWT authentication for WebSocket connections using subprotocol header.

**Current Issue:**
WebSocket connections for log streaming don't support custom HTTP headers like 'Authorization'.

**CORRECTED Solution:**
Use WebSocket Subprotocol with token embedded in protocol name.

**Frontend Implementation (UPDATED):**
```javascript
const protocol = `access_token.${token}`;
const ws = new WebSocket(wsUrl, protocol);
// Browser sends: Sec-WebSocket-Protocol: access_token.<jwt_token>
```

**Backend Requirements (CORRECTED):**

1. **Extract token from subprotocol header:**
   - Read 'Sec-WebSocket-Protocol' header during WebSocket upgrade
   - Protocol format: `access_token.<jwt_token>`
   - Split on first '.' to separate prefix from token
   - Example: `access_token.eyJhbGc...` → prefix=`access_token`, token=`eyJhbGc...`

2. **Validate JWT token:**
   - Use existing JWT validation middleware/function
   - Verify token signature and expiration
   - Extract user claims (userId, role)
   - Return 401 if token invalid/missing

3. **Accept connection:**
   - If token valid: Accept upgrade with `Sec-WebSocket-Protocol: access_token` (just the prefix, NOT the token\!)
   - If token invalid: Reject with HTTP 401 Unauthorized
   - Apply same RBAC rules as REST endpoints

4. **Endpoint affected:**
   - WS /api/v1/scenarios/run/{scenarioRunName}/jobs/{jobId}/logs

**Example Go Implementation (gorilla/websocket):**
```go
// Read the Sec-WebSocket-Protocol header
protocols := r.Header.Get("Sec-WebSocket-Protocol")
if protocols == "" {
    http.Error(w, "Missing Sec-WebSocket-Protocol", 401)
    return
}

// Parse protocol: "access_token.<jwt>"
parts := strings.SplitN(protocols, ".", 2)
if len(parts) \!= 2 || parts[0] \!= "access_token" {
    http.Error(w, "Invalid protocol format", 401)
    return
}

token := parts[1]

// Validate JWT token
claims, err := validateJWT(token)
if err \!= nil {
    http.Error(w, "Invalid token", 401)
    return
}

// Upgrade with ONLY the prefix (not the full token\!)
upgrader := websocket.Upgrader{
    Subprotocols: []string{"access_token"},
}

conn, err := upgrader.Upgrade(w, r, http.Header{
    "Sec-WebSocket-Protocol": []string{"access_token"},
})
if err \!= nil {
    return
}

// Connection established with authenticated user
// Use claims.UserId, claims.Role for authorization
```

**Security Notes:**
- Token never appears in URL, query params, or server logs

title: [krknctl] Add build tags for optional GPU support and adopt beads
description:
## Context
krknctl currently has a hard dependency on github.com/NVIDIA/go-nvml which requires CGO.
This forces all consumers (krkn-operator, krkn-operator-console, krkn-operator-acm) to use workarounds.

## Current workaround in krkn-operator
- Created local stub in hack/stub-nvml/
- Added replace directive in go.mod
- Works but requires maintenance in every consuming project

## Proposed solution for krknctl

### Part 1: GPU support with build tags
Refactor GPU detection to use build tags:

**File: pkg/gpudetect/detector_gpu.go**
```go
//go:build gpu

package gpudetect

import "github.com/NVIDIA/go-nvml/pkg/nvml"

// Real GPU detection implementation
func DetectGPUs() ([]GPU, error) {
    // ... existing nvml code ...
}
```

**File: pkg/gpudetect/detector_nogpu.go**
```go
//go:build !gpu

package gpudetect

// Stub implementation for builds without GPU support
func DetectGPUs() ([]GPU, error) {
    return []GPU{}, nil // No GPUs detected
}
```

### Build behavior
- `go build` (default) → No CGO, no GPU support, pure Go binary
- `go build -tags gpu` → CGO enabled, full GPU support

### Benefits
✅ Default builds work without CGO (more portable)
✅ All consumers (operator/console/ACM) benefit
✅ GPU support becomes opt-in instead of required
✅ Centralized maintenance in krknctl
✅ No replace directives needed in consuming projects

### Part 2: Adopt beads for task tracking
krknctl should adopt beads for issue tracking to align with ecosystem projects.

**Setup steps:**
1. Symlink .beads to central database: `ln -s ~/Projects/beads/.beads .beads`
2. Create PROJECT.toml with beads.project_label = "project:krknctl"
3. Configure git hooks for auto-export
4. Create CLAUDE.md referencing central config (like krkn-operator)

**Benefits:**
✅ Unified issue tracking across ecosystem
✅ Cross-project dependencies visible (e.g. operator blocked by krknctl feature)
✅ Shared workflow with operator/console/ACM
✅ Issues survive git history via beads/ exports

## After krknctl implements this
In krkn-operator:
1. Remove hack/stub-nvml/
2. Remove replace directive from go.mod
3. Update go.mod to latest krknctl version
4. Run go mod vendor
5. Verify builds work without workarounds

- krkn-operator uses stub until krknctl ships fix

title: Security: public files/workflows writable by any authenticated user

- UpdateWorkflow/DeleteWorkflow use canAccessFile() for permission check

- Apply to both file_handlers.go and workflow_handlers.go

**Refactoring approach**:

```go
// Helper function
func testRoleMiddleware(t *testing.T, tg *TokenGenerator, middleware func(http.Handler) http.Handler, tests []testCase) {
    for _, tt := range tests {
        t.Run(tt.name, func(t *testing.T) {
            token, err := tg.GenerateToken("[email protected]", tt.userRole, "Test", "User", "Org")
            if err != nil {
                t.Fatalf("Failed to generate token: %v", err)
            }
            
            handlerCalled := false
            testHandler := http.HandlerFunc(func(w http.ResponseWriter, r *http.Request) {
                handlerCalled = true
                w.WriteHeader(http.StatusOK)
            })
            
            handler := RequireAuth(middleware(testHandler))
            
            req := httptest.NewRequest("GET", "/test", nil)
            req.Header.Set("Authorization", "Bearer "+token)
            w := httptest.NewRecorder()
            
            handler.ServeHTTP(w, req)
            
            if w.Code != tt.expectedStatus {
                t.Errorf("Expected status %d, got %d", tt.expectedStatus, w.Code)
            }
            
            if handlerCalled != tt.expectCalled {
                t.Errorf("Expected handler called=%v, got %v", tt.expectCalled, handlerCalled)
            }
        })
    }
}
```

title: Hub.Broadcast blocking send can stall informers
description:
Hub.Broadcast does blocking send into buffered broadcast channel.

Watcher event handlers call broadcasts synchronously. Under bursty updates
this can block informer callbacks and delay cache/event processing.

Current code:
func (h *Hub) Broadcast(...) {
    h.broadcast <- &BroadcastMessage{...}  // BLOCKING
}

Impact:
- Under burst: informer OnUpdate/OnAdd handlers block waiting for Hub
- Slows down cache sync and event processing
- Could cause event queue buildup

Fix options:
1. Non-blocking send with select/default (drop on full)
2. Increase buffer size (256 → 1024+)
3. Async goroutine per broadcast (overhead)

Recommend: #1 (non-blocking with warning log on drop)

Impact: MEDIUM - reliability under load
close_reason: Broadcasts now non-blocking with select/default. Drops on full channel prevent informer stalls. Logged at V(1).
